To keep from littering this conversation with replies to each comment, I'm consolidating. Below you remark that bad conditions are anathema and should be reported to federal authorities. Problematically, the USDA has been gutted in terms of budget and personnel and if they had the reach necessary to control a lot of what happens in factory animal husbandry ("Concentrated Animal Feed Operations") I'm sure they would. But they can't. Lots of terrible conditions are never addressed and we would be remarkably naive if we were to think that Tyson, Cargill and Swift don't grease a lot of palms to be permitted to cut corners. Worse, when they are fined for terrible practices, such fines are more or less the cost of doing business because such fines seldom affect the bottom line. Running the risk of fines and then receiving them is cheaper than avoiding the practices that would be fined.

American food has demonstrably suffered since we have decided to engage in CAFO, corporation-owned food production. Eggs are now salmonella in a shell. Many young people don't recall when people could eat raw eggs, order a soft-boiled egg from a menu without reading the warning about undercooked eggs, but salmonella contamination of our egg supply is recent and not something that continental Europe even worries about. I don't think chronic staph infections in meat are even on European radars.

Grass-fed beef is more nutritious. Chickens permitted to peck and scratch for food produce healthier eggs than vegetarian caged hens. Smaller farms with smaller, localized slaughter seldom have e.coli or salmonella contaminated meats and when it happens controlling the outbreak is much easier than when we have to have multi-state or national recalls. And CAFOs effects on local environments are unavoidable - entire water systems have been wrecked for generations due to manure run off. The very air becomes toxic.

My family were cattle farmers. What happens now in dairy farms and "ranches" is unrecognizable to what my grandfather did 50 years ago. Our food is less nutritious, is often tainted and we think it's okay as long as we don't have to pay much for the meat. Europeans pay more for meat and they get more because their animals are fed appropriate foods and are slaughtered in sensible manners. The way Americans produce and process meats is as unhealthy as any other part of our food economy and we accept it because we really do think that the federal government has it all under control. It's not the case and since we don't have bottom line nutritional values required for meats and dairy we eat, even untainted meats and dairy are not as healthful as they were when I was a little girl.

Is it better to have substandard product as long as it is affordable for all people? I can't necessarily answer that because I can afford the better product and therefore have a "privileged" mindset. But it's tempting to think about a nation wherein we didn't waste our money on a continual diet of nutritionally-deficient foods and instead funneled that money into better foods. Not being a food snob - an occasional hamburger or hot dog or twinkie is fun. But the increased reliance on fast food has demanded extremely low food prices to be able to give value meals and similar and has contributed more than any other consumer factor to CAFOs. It's not your preference for corn-fed beef or my preference for wild salmon (farm salmon can literally kill me due to the extraordinarily high level of histamines in it but that's an issue for another time) that dictates the current animal husbandry operations in the USA - it's corporations that buy and turn the product into a branded foodstuff like Big Macs or McNuggets. Corporations call the tune and until we wrench control of all that we eat back from companies that have no interest in our health or well-being, all of this conversation is moot because we have zero control over any of this. Our dollars and interests dictate nothing and the government does not have our back.
